qs.q: A medical student accidentally inhales mold spores of Aspergillus fumigatus in the lab. Which primary innate immune cell type is chiefly responsible for clearing these inhaled conidia from a healthy lung?
qs.e: Alveolar macrophages phagocytose small conidia, while recruited neutrophils attack larger hyphal elements that escape clearance.

qs.q: A lab technician ingests grains contaminated with Aspergillus flavus secondary metabolites. Which primary biochemical mechanism underlies the acute hepatotoxicity of this ingested mycotoxin?
o: Epoxide formation leading to DNA adducts
qs.e: Aflatoxin B1 is metabolized into a reactive epoxide intermediate that binds guanine bases, causing DNA damage and necrosis.

qs.q: A patient with chronic granulomatous disease develops an invasive fungal infection characterized by septate hyphae branching at acute angles. Which neutrophil defect predisposes this patient to Aspergillus invasion?
o: Impaired degranulation of myeloperoxidase enzymes in cells
Defective phagolysosome acidification in circulating monocytes
Absence of surface complement receptors on circulating cells
Inability to generate reactive oxygen species via NADPH oxidase
Inadequate integrin expression required for vascular rolling
qs.e: NADPH oxidase deficiency prevents neutrophils from producing oxidative metabolites needed to kill engulfed hyphal fungal elements.

qs.q: A patient is diagnosed with an invasive Aspergillus infection and is started on voriconazole. Which distinctive visual side effect occurs frequently in patients taking this specific antifungal agent?
o: Irreversible corneal opacification with progressive stromal scarring
Severe acute bilateral angle‑closure glaucoma attacks
Complete bilateral loss of peripheral visual fields and perception
Marked constriction of retinal arterioles leading to pallor
Transient visual disturbances such as photopsia and blurred vision
qs.e: Voriconazole frequently causes transient, reversible visual disturbances such as altered light perception, photopsia, and blurred vision.

qs.q: Which statement regarding aspergillosis is correct? Aspergillus causes a wide range of local infections (otomycosis, keratitis, onychomycosis, sinusitis) beyond invasive pulmonary disease; blood cultures are usually negative even in invasive disease, so c is false. ---
o: Clinical manifestations include local infections of the ear and sinuses
Bone marrow transplant recipients are not at risk for invasive disease
Patients on parenteral corticosteroids are not at risk for invasive disease
Pulmonary aspergillosis is frequently diagnosed by culturing blood samples
Patients with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis rarely have eosinophilia
qs.e: Aspergillus species frequently cause localized infections involving the ear, cornea, nails, and sinuses in addition to pulmonary manifestations.

qs.q: A neonate has tetany, a heart murmur, serum calcium of 6.3 mg/dL, and a VSD. Over the first year he develops Pneumocystis, Aspergillus, and viral upper respiratory infections. Most likely explanation?
o: Failure of B-cell plasma cell maturation
qs.e: Hypocalcemia (absent parathyroids) + cardiac defects + T-cell deficiency causing fungal and viral infections = DiGeorge syndrome. Chromosome 22q11 deletion causes failure of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouch development → absent thymus and parathyroids.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Aspergillus is a ubiquitous mold that can cause invasive disease in immunocompromised hosts and allergic disease in healthy lungs. Diagnosis relies on imaging, antigen tests, and culture, while treatment centers on voriconazole or amphotericin B with adjunctive surgery when needed.

sections.p: Aspergillus species are filamentous fungi found in soil and decaying organic matter. They produce airborne spores that can be inhaled, leading to a spectrum of pulmonary disease.
The mold forms septate hyphae with acute-angle branching. Some species produce aflatoxins, potent carcinogens.
Spores are released into air from decaying vegetation. Inhalation is the main route; spores can also contaminate food.
Invasive aspergillosis (IA) occurs in neutropenic or transplant patients; allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) affects asthmatics; aspergilloma forms in pre‑existing lung cavities.
Diagnosis integrates clinical, radiologic, serologic, and microbiologic data.

t.b: Detects nodules, halo sign, air‑filled cavities; a halo sign suggests early IA.
Positive in IA; a serial rise predicts treatment failure.
Positive in chronic pulmonary aspergillosis and aspergilloma.
Rapid detection; useful when culture is negative.
